5-gestes-reduire-empreinte-carbone-cuisi.title: 5 actions to cut your kitchen's carbon footprint
5-gestes-reduire-empreinte-carbone-cuisi.excerpt: From supplier selection to waste management, discover how to act effectively in your restaurant.
5-gestes-reduire-empreinte-carbone-cuisi.content:
## The carbon footprint is also decided in the kitchen

Food accounts for about 25% of a French household's carbon footprint (source: ADEME). Here are five high-impact actions, ranked by real effectiveness.

## 1. Rebalance your proteins

The number one lever, by far. Replacing a beef meal with pulses saves around 25 kg CO2e per kilo of protein. Chickpeas, lentils, quinoa: organic plant proteins are also the cheapest per kilo of protein.

## 2. Hunt down food waste

30 kg of food thrown away per person per year in France, including 7 kg still in its packaging. Planning menus and cooking leftovers saves more CO2 than all the other actions combined — and money too.

## 3. Favour sea freight over air freight

A kilo of product imported by plane emits ~37 times more than by ship (ADEME factors: 0.602 vs 0.016 kg CO2e/t.km). Coffee, cocoa and spices travel very well by sea. Beware of ultra-perishable exotic fresh produce: it often travels by plane.

## 4. Choose seasonal products

A tomato grown in a heated greenhouse in January emits up to 10 times more than the same tomato in summer. The seasonal calendar remains the simplest tool.

## 5. Reduce packaging

Bulk and large formats: on EthiMarket, products offering bulk or compostable packaging can be filtered (the "packaging" facet of the search engine).

**The bottom line**: it is the structural choices (proteins, waste, transport mode) that matter — not perfection on the details.

agriculture-bio-nourrir-10-milliards.title: Can organic farming feed 10 billion people?
agriculture-bio-nourrir-10-milliards.excerpt: A review of yields, costs and challenges. Is the organic transition viable on a global scale?
agriculture-bio-nourrir-10-milliards.content:
## The awkward question

Organic farming has yields 8 to 25% lower depending on the crop (meta-analyses Seufert et al. 2012, Ponisio et al. 2015). So can it feed a humanity approaching 10 billion?

## What the research says

The reference study (Muller et al. 2017, Nature Communications) answers: **yes, under three conditions**. A large-scale shift to organic could feed the planet if we simultaneously reduce food waste (a third of global production), the share of crops dedicated to animal feed, and the consumption of animal products.

## The real problem is not yield

We already produce enough to feed 10 billion people. Hunger is a problem of distribution, waste and economic access — not of global volume. Organic farming, with slightly lower yields but living soils and preserved biodiversity, fits into a systemic equation.

## And for producers in the Global South?

For smallholders, organic often means better income (price premium, less dependence on imported inputs) and better climate resilience. EthiMarket's partner cooperatives can testify: certification is an economic lever as much as an ecological one.

## An honest conclusion

Organic alone will not "save" global food. Combined with waste reduction and dietary change, it is a credible pillar — and the most solid one for long-term soil health.

certification-bio-guide-producteurs.title: Organic certification: the complete guide for producers
certification-bio-guide-producteurs.excerpt: Everything you need to know to obtain organic certification: procedures, costs, bodies, timelines and pitfalls to avoid.
certification-bio-guide-producteurs.content:
## The certification journey made clear

Obtaining organic certification is an investment: expect 12 to 36 months of conversion and an annual audit. Here is the typical journey for a producer.

## 1. Choose your standard and your body

EU Organic (Regulation 2018/848) to sell in Europe, USDA Organic for the United States, JAS for Japan. Accredited certification bodies (Ecocert, Control Union, Kiwa BCS, Africert…) operate in most producing countries.

## 2. The conversion period

2 to 3 years during which practices must be 100% organic but the production cannot yet be sold as such. It is the hardest period financially — some buyers (including several on EthiMarket) value "in conversion" products.

## 3. The initial audit

Inspection of plots, stocks and input-output accounting. The auditor checks the absence of prohibited inputs and the strict separation of organic and non-organic.

## 4. The certificate and its scope

The certificate specifies the covered products, the areas, and its validity date (usually 12 months). **The certificate number is public**: any buyer can verify it with the body.

## 5. Annual renewal

A follow-up audit every year, plus unannounced checks. An expired certificate = no more organic sales, immediately.

## EthiMarket's advice

Upload your certificate as soon as your products go online: the team verifies it with your body and your page displays "✅ Certified" — the most powerful sales argument with professional buyers.

choisir-fournisseurs-bio-5-etapes.title: How to choose your organic suppliers in 5 steps
choisir-fournisseurs-bio-5-etapes.excerpt: A practical method to identify, evaluate and select the best organic suppliers for your business.
choisir-fournisseurs-bio-5-etapes.content:
## Why vetting your suppliers changes everything

Choosing an organic supplier is not just about comparing prices. An expired certificate, an opaque supply chain or questionable social conditions can cost far more than a few cents per kilo: product recalls, reputational damage, CSRD non-compliance.

## Step 1 — Demand proof, not promises

Systematically ask for the certificate number, the issuing body and the validity date. A serious supplier provides them within minutes. On EthiMarket, this information is published on every product page and verified with the bodies.

## Step 2 — Assess real traceability

Batch number, production GPS coordinates, harvest dates: without these elements, it is impossible to trace back the chain in case of a problem. Beware of suppliers who document up to the processor but not down to the farm.

## Step 3 — Audit social conditions

Living wage, absence of child labour, recent social audit (SA8000, BSCI). A structured cooperative is often a better signal than an anonymous trader.

## Step 4 — Test with a sample then a small batch

Order a sample, then a first batch at the MOQ. Evaluate quality, delivery reliability and communication before committing volumes.

## Step 5 — Put it in writing

Prices, lead times, offer validity, certificate renewal conditions: everything must be recorded. EthiMarket's quote module timestamps every step for you.

**In short**: proof before promise. A good organic supplier has nothing to hide — and everything to document.

fairtrade-vs-rainforest-alliance.title: Fairtrade vs Rainforest Alliance: the differences
fairtrade-vs-rainforest-alliance.excerpt: Two major fair trade labels, but very different approaches. A breakdown to make the right choice.
fairtrade-vs-rainforest-alliance.content:
## Two labels, two philosophies

Fairtrade (Max Havelaar) and Rainforest Alliance are the two certifications most requested by European buyers. They do not guarantee the same things.

## Fairtrade: price first

The heart of the Fairtrade system is economic: a **guaranteed minimum price** for the producer, whatever the volatility of market prices, plus a **development premium** paid to the cooperative for collective projects (schools, access to water, equipment). The standard also prohibits child labour and imposes democratic governance criteria for cooperatives. Certification is carried by FLO-CERT, which audits producer organisations.

## Rainforest Alliance: ecosystem first

Rainforest Alliance (merged with UTZ in 2018) focuses on **sustainable agriculture**: forest protection, biodiversity preservation, water and soil management, decent working conditions. There is no guaranteed minimum price, but a "sustainability differential" paid to the producer.

## How to choose as a buyer?

- Your priority is the **economic security of producers** → Fairtrade.
- Your priority is **environmental impact and deforestation** (cocoa, coffee) → Rainforest Alliance.
- The two can be combined: many cooperatives hold both certifications.

## Verify, always

Whatever the label, demand a valid certificate. On EthiMarket, the status of each certification (verified with the body, in progress, or mere declaration) is public on the product page.

negociation-obtenir-meilleurs-prix-bio.title: Negotiation: getting the best organic prices
negociation-obtenir-meilleurs-prix-bio.excerpt: Techniques and strategies to negotiate effectively with your organic suppliers without sacrificing quality.
negociation-obtenir-meilleurs-prix-bio.content:
## Negotiating in organic B2B: price is not the only lever

Getting a good price without strangling your supplier is possible — and it is the only sustainable strategy. Here are the levers that work.

## Lever 1: volume and regularity

Volume discount grids reward volume, but **regularity** is often worth more than a one-off large volume: a producer who can plan production grants better terms. Offer a quarterly or annual commitment.

## Lever 2: seasonality

Order during harvest season (when stocks are full) rather than at the end of the season. Harvest dates are displayed on EthiMarket product pages.

## Lever 3: fast payment

For a cooperative, cash flow is vital. Payment on receipt (rather than at 60 days) justifies a 2 to 5% discount — everyone wins.

## Lever 4: the "on quote" tiers

Beyond the last public tier, everything is negotiable: grouped logistics, simplified packaging, direct pickup. That is where the real savings are made.

## What NOT to negotiate

A price below the sustainable cost of production. A squeezed supplier always compensates somewhere: quality, social conditions, or they disappear — and you start your sourcing from scratch. Your quote acceptance rate and the health of your suppliers are part of your procurement performance.

**The EthiMarket reflex**: use the comparator's justification sheet to argue a supplier choice to your management — including when it is not the cheapest one.

permaculture-revolution-douce-champs.title: Permaculture: a gentle revolution in our fields
permaculture-revolution-douce-champs.excerpt: Permaculture is gaining ground. How this regenerative approach is transforming agriculture and restoring soils.
permaculture-revolution-douce-champs.content:
## Permaculture leaves the garden

Long confined to activist vegetable plots, permaculture now inspires entire commercial farms. Its principle: designing agricultural systems that mimic natural ecosystems — diversity, layering, recycling of matter.

## Three principles that change production

**1. Never leave soil bare.** Permanent cover crops and mulching: the soil regenerates instead of eroding.

**2. Combine rather than separate.** Layered crops (trees + shrubs + ground cover), beneficial associations. This is the agroforestry principle practised by the Yirgacheffe coffee growers.

**3. Close the loops.** Compost, water retention, hedges: the farm produces its own fertility.

## Measured results

Well-run permaculture farms achieve remarkable productivity per hectare on small areas (INRAE study on the Bec Hellouin farm), with biodiversity 3 to 5 times higher than neighbouring conventional plots.

## What it changes for buyers

A product from agroforestry or permaculture systems generally carries a lower carbon footprint and precise plot-level traceability. On EthiMarket, the production method is documented on every page — search for "agroforestry" or "permaculture" in the engine.

portrait-fatima-benali-argan-atlas.title: Meeting Fatima Benali, president of the Argan Atlas cooperative
portrait-fatima-benali-argan-atlas.excerpt: For 20 years, she has been transforming the lives of 80 Berber women through organic argan oil. The story of a fight for economic independence.
portrait-fatima-benali-argan-atlas.content:
## One president, 64 members

In Essaouira, Fatima Benali has chaired the Argan Atlas cooperative since 2015. "When we started, we sold our oil to middlemen who paid a third of its value. Today, we export directly and every woman in the cooperative is a co-owner."

## Know-how passed from mother to daughter

The cooperative's argan oil comes from certified organic wild harvesting. The cracking of the nuts remains manual — a skill handed down from generation to generation. "Full mechanisation would break the kernel and degrade the oil. Our method is slower, but it is what makes the quality."

## What direct trade has changed

Since switching to direct sales: members' incomes have risen by 60%, the cooperative has funded a nursery and literacy classes, and the fair trade premium paid for a collection vehicle.

"Buyers who visit us always ask the same questions: are your certificates valid? Who monitors your working conditions? That is exactly what should be asked. A serious cooperative has the answers."

## Verifiable, as always

Argan Atlas's Organic (Ecocert) and Fair Trade (FLO-CERT) certifications are verified and published on the cooperative's shop, with certificate numbers and validity dates.

saffron-fields-iran-renaissance-safran.title: Saffron Fields Iran: the rebirth of ancestral saffron
saffron-fields-iran-renaissance-safran.excerpt: On the Iranian highlands, a cooperative is reviving the thousand-year-old culture of saffron with organic methods.
saffron-fields-iran-renaissance-safran.content:
## Saffron, the red gold of Kermanshah

Three generations of the same family grow saffron on the Kermanshah plateaus in Iran. Saffron Fields perpetuates a demanding method: flowers harvested at dawn, hand-trimmed the same day, gentle traditional drying.

## Why dawn?

Crocus sativus opens at sunrise. Harvested before fully opening, the flowers protect the stigmas from oxidation — this is what preserves the aromatic power. It takes about 150,000 flowers for one kilo of dry saffron.

## The Negin grade

Saffron Fields only sells Negin grade: whole stigmas, deep red, without yellow style. Every batch is tested in an independent laboratory (crocin, picrocrocin, safranal — ISO 3632 standard).

## The challenges of an Iranian producer

Between logistical constraints and currency fluctuations, exporting from Iran requires resilience. Direct trade through transparent platforms allows the family to be rewarded for quality rather than suffering middlemen's prices.

"Our saffron carries one hundred and fifty years of family history. What we ask of buyers is to judge on the analyses and the quality — they speak for themselves."

yirgacheffe-coffee-union-ethiopie.title: Yirgacheffe Coffee Union: 187 Ethiopian families
yirgacheffe-coffee-union-ethiopie.excerpt: Portrait of an emblematic cooperative exporting its exceptional coffee worldwide through direct trade.
yirgacheffe-coffee-union-ethiopie.content:
## 187 families, 14 cooperatives, an exceptional terroir

The Yirgacheffe Coffee Union has federated the coffee cooperatives of the Yirgacheffe region in Ethiopia — the historical birthplace of arabica — since 2005. Altitude: 1,900 metres. Varieties: local heirlooms, grown under shade.

## Agroforestry as a heritage

Here, coffee grows under the canopy, mixed with enset and acacia trees. This agroforestry system preserves biodiversity, protects the soils and gives the coffee its characteristic floral notes. It also captures carbon — shade-grown coffee's footprint is among the lowest in the industry.

## Washing stations in producers' hands

The union runs its own washing and drying stations, which allows it to control quality end-to-end and capture the added value of processing. Direct export, without traders, has increased member families' income by more than 40% since 2018.

## Full traceability

Every exported batch carries a number, the washing station of origin and the GPS coordinates of the collection area. The Organic and Rainforest Alliance certifications are audited every year.

On EthiMarket, the union's Yirgacheffe coffee is one of the best documented products: verified certificates, traced batch, published GPS.
